alignment.note: The Vulgate transmits an entirely different verse (Mark 9:11, concerning Elijah's coming), representing a textual dislocation or manuscript error. Greek and Peshitta both attest Mark 9:10 (keeping the word about rising from the dead), while the Vulgate has imported the subsequent verse's content here.

Greek uses prepositional phrase πρὸς ἑαυτοὺς with participle συζητοῦντες ('among themselves, questioning'); Peshitta employs the reflexive prepositional phrase ܒܢܦܫܗܘܢ ('in their souls/selves') as a single locution, achieving the same semantic force with different syntax.

Peshitta adds the periphrastic construction ܘܒܥܝܢ ܗܘܘ ('and they were seeking/asking'), making explicit the durative aspect of the disciples' questioning that Greek conveys through the present participle συζητοῦντες alone.
Greek τί ἐστιν ('what is') follows standard Greek interrogative word order; Peshitta ܕܡܢܐ ܗܝ ('what [is] it') inverts to Semitic VSO pattern with feminine copula ܗܝ agreeing with ܡܠܬܐ ('word').

Peshitta expands Greek articular infinitive τὸ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῆναι into full nominal clause ܗܕܐ ܡܠܬܐ ('this word'), making explicit the referent of the interrogative and creating a more elaborate Semitic construction.

Greek uses articular infinitive construction τὸ ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῆναι ('the rising from the dead'); Peshitta employs temporal clause ܕܡܐ ܕܩܡ ܡܢ ܒܝܬ ܡܝܬܐ ('when he rises from the house of the dead'), substituting the idiomatic ܒܝܬ ܡܝܬܐ (lit. 'house of the dead') for simple 'from the dead' and recasting the infinitive as finite verb.

The entire Vulgate text represents Mark 9:11 ('And they asked him, saying: Why then do the Pharisees and scribes say that Elijah must come first?'), not Mark 9:10. This constitutes a complete verse substitution, likely due to manuscript confusion, scribal error, or early Latin textual tradition divergence.
